# fluent-sdfx

> A fluent, chainable Go API over [sdfx](https://github.com/snowbldr/sdfx), a signed-distance-function CAD kernel. Build parts by composing primitives, transforms and booleans on two immutable types: `*shape.Shape` (2D) and `*solid.Solid` (3D). Angles are degrees, lengths are millimetres, Z is up.

This file is the reference for a model (or a person) writing fluent-sdfx code. It is the short one: the mental model, the conventions that must not be guessed, the traps that have actually cost parts, and how to verify work before claiming it. The companion `llms-api.txt` is generated from the source and lists every exported symbol with its signature and doc synopsis; load it when you need a signature or want to know whether something exists. Every claim in this file was checked by probing the code, not by reading it; where the code surprised the author, that surprise is written down.

If you take away one thing: **a fluent-sdfx program is one expression that describes the part.** Every operation returns a new value, so `solid.Cylinder(20, 10, 1).Cut(...).RotateZ(45).STL("out.stl", 5)` is the natural style. Do not write a sequence of statements that mutate a builder.

## Mental model

- **Two core types.** `*shape.Shape` wraps `sdf.SDF2`; `*solid.Solid` wraps `sdf.SDF3`. Both are immutable: every method returns a new value and never modifies its receiver.
- **The field is the truth.** A solid is a function from a point to a signed distance: negative inside material, positive in air, zero on the surface. Anything you want to know about a part can be asked of that function at a point, and the `validate` package exists to ask it well. The mesh is a rendering of the field, not the part.
- **Degrees everywhere, with two exceptions.** Every angle parameter is degrees (`RotateZ(45)`, `TwistExtrude(20, 90)`, `PressureAngleDeg`). The exceptions are `p2.RT(r, theta)` and `PolyVertex.Polar()`, which take radians.
- **Z is up, and every axial thing uses Z.** Cylinders, cones, screws, helices, `Revolve` and the `RotateCopyZ` pattern all take Z as their axis. For `Revolve`, the 2D profile lives in the XY plane: profile +X is the radius from the axis and profile Y becomes world Z.
- **Constructors panic on nonsense, mostly.** No `(*Shape, error)` tuples; a negative sphere radius, an empty `UnionAll`, a `Box` round larger than half a side, or a non-positive `PyramidFrustum` dimension panics. But a negative `Cone` radius and a negative `Rect` size are silently accepted. Do not rely on a panic to catch a bad number; probe the result.
- **2D becomes 3D** through `.Extrude`, `.ExtrudeRounded`, `.TwistExtrude`, `.ScaleExtrude`, `.Revolve`, `.LoftTo`, `.SweepHelix`, `.Screw`. **3D becomes 2D** through `shape.SliceAt(solid, plane)`, which returns a `*shape.Shape`. (`Solid.SliceAt` returns a raw `sdf.SDF2`; wrap it with `shape.Wrap2D` if you call it.)
- **No build tool, no DSL.** Each part is a `package main` whose `main` ends in `.STL(path, cellsPerMM)`.

## Conventions that must not be guessed

These are the facts a person leaves implicit and a model gets wrong. Each was verified by evaluating the field.

- **Primitives are centred on the origin**: `Box`, `Cylinder`, `Sphere`, `Cone`, `Capsule`, `Torus`, `Rect`, `Circle`, and every extrusion (`Extrude(h)` spans z = -h/2 .. +h/2). The one that is not: `PyramidFrustum` sits on z = 0. Use `.ZeroZ()` to put a part on the build plate and `.BottomAt(z)` to put its bottom at a height.
- **Anchor names are axis directions.** Front = -Y, Back = +Y, Left = -X, Right = +X, Bottom = -Z, Top = +Z. So `FrontAt(y)` pins the **minimum-Y** face at y and `BackAt(y)` the maximum-Y face. This trap bit three separate agents in one project; if you are unsure, probe with `validate.At`.
- **Rotations follow the right-hand rule about the world axis, in degrees.** `RotateX(90)` sends +Y to +Z and +Z to -Y. `RotateY(90)` sends +Z to +X and +X to -Z. `RotateZ(90)` sends +X to +Y and +Y to -X. `RotateAxis` normalises its axis for you.
- **Scale is about the world origin, not the part.** `Scale` and `ScaleUniform` move a part that is not at the origin as well as resize it (a box centred at x = 10 scaled ×2 lands at x = 20). Scale in the part's own frame first, then position, or accept the move.
- **Mirror naming differs between 2D and 3D.** 3D names the plane: `MirrorXY` flips Z, `MirrorXZ` flips Y, `MirrorYZ` flips X. 2D names the line: `Shape.MirrorX` reflects across the X axis and therefore **flips Y**; `Shape.MirrorY` flips X.
- **Variadic booleans union their arguments first.** `a.Cut(b, c)` is `a - (b ∪ c)`, which is what you want. `a.Intersect(b, c)` is `a ∩ (b ∪ c)`, which is usually **not**: for the common volume of three solids, chain `a.Intersect(b).Intersect(c)`.
- **`Multi` places copies at the given offsets only**, none at the origin. `Array` starts at the receiver; `layout.Grid` is centred on the origin.
- **Field values are distances only near simple geometry.** After booleans, twists, scale-extrudes and `Correct`, the field is a bound: the sign is always right, the magnitude can understate the distance. Ask the field "inside or outside", and use the surface-finding helpers when you need a measurement.

## Constructor cheat-sheet

```go
// 3D primitives — all centred on the origin unless noted
solid.Box(v3.XYZ(20, 16, 10), 1.5)   // size, edge round
solid.Cylinder(20, 10, 1)             // height, radius, edge round; axis Z
solid.Sphere(12)
solid.Cone(18, 10, 4, 0.5)            // height, bottom radius, top radius, round
solid.Capsule(20, 6)                  // OVERALL length end to end (the cylinder body is 20 - 2*6 = 8), radius
solid.Torus(12, 3)                    // major (ring centre) radius, minor radius
solid.PyramidFrustum(8, 5, 12)        // half-base, half-top, height; SITS ON z=0; either end may be the wider one
solid.Gyroid(...).WithBounds(box)     // Gyroid has a zero bounding box; WithBounds is the only way to render it

// 2D primitives — centred on the origin
shape.Rect(v2.XY(30, 20), 3)          // size, corner round
shape.Circle(15)
shape.Hole(6)                         // a circle given its DIAMETER: holes are specified as diameters, so the halving happens here
shape.Polygon([]v2.Vec{...})          // either winding order is fine
shape.Hexagon(12)                     // CIRCUMradius (centre to vertex), a vertex on +X; across-flats = 12*sqrt(3)
shape.Triangle(10)                    // equilateral, inscribed radius 10, apex on +Y, flat base at y = -5
shape.Star(15, 7, 5)                  // outer, inner, points; tips exactly at outer, first tip on +X, sharp corners
shape.Cross(10, 2)                    // two bars: length, thickness
shape.Text(font, "hello", 10)         // needs shape.LoadFont(path); call .Cache() on the result before reusing it

// Polygon builder (corner-by-corner, with fillets and chamfers)
p := shape.NewPoly()
p.Add(0, 0)
p.Add(10, 0).Smooth(2, 6)             // fillet this corner: radius 2, 6 facets
p.Add(10, 5).Chamfer(1)
p.Add(12, 8).Arc(3, 8)                // arc to this vertex: positive bulges outward, negative curves inward
p.Close()
profile := p.Build()

// Bezier builder: NewBezier() alone is unusable — handles are set on each vertex
b := shape.NewBezier()
b.Add(0, 0).HandleFwd(45, 3)          // tangent angle (degrees) and handle length
b.Add(10, 10).Handle(0, 3, 3)         // angle, forward length, reverse length
b.Close()
curve := b.Build()

// Vectors
v3.XYZ(1, 2, 3)   v3.X(5)   v3.YZ(2, 3)   v3.Zero
v2.XY(10, 20)
p2.RT(r, theta)   // theta in RADIANS — the one place they are used
```

## 2D to 3D cheat-sheet

```go
profile.Extrude(8)                            // z = -4..+4
profile.ExtrudeRounded(8, 1.5)                // rounds the top and bottom edges AND grows the footprint by 1.5 on every side
profile.TwistExtrude(20, 90)                  // twist in degrees over the height
profile.ScaleExtrude(20, v2.XY(0.4, 0.4))     // scales the profile PROPORTIONALLY toward the top (not a uniform inset)
bottom.LoftTo(top, height, round)             // interpolates the two fields; exact on-axis, corners pull in slightly
profile.Revolve()                             // full turn about Z; profile +X = radius, profile Y -> world Z
profile.RevolveAngle(270)                     // partial turn, degrees; note its bbox is the full-circle envelope
profile.SweepHelix(radius, turns, height, flatEnds)
profile.Screw(height, start, pitch, starts)   // starts = 1 for a normal thread
```

Choosing between the tapered ones matters. `ScaleExtrude` scales the profile about its centre, so a 20×10 rectangle with a "2 mm inset" is off by 0.25 mm in Y. `LoftTo` between two explicit profiles is exact on the axes and about 0.3 mm short at corners because it interpolates fields. For a square frustum use `PyramidFrustum`, which is exact; for a chamfer band on a rectangular plate, `CutPlane` four times is exact.

`SweepHelix`'s last argument reads backwards. `flatEnds=false` gives flat horizontal slices at z = ±height/2, total height exactly `height`. `flatEnds=true` gives full profile cross-sections cut perpendicular to the sweep, which **overhang** the end planes by up to the profile radius. If you want the rib to end flush with the part, pass `false`.

## Boolean cheat-sheet

```go
a.Union(b, c, d)                  // variadic; Add is an alias
a.Cut(tool1, tool2, tool3)        // variadic: a - (t1 ∪ t2 ∪ t3); Difference is an alias
a.Intersect(b)                    // ONE argument; a.Intersect(b, c) means a ∩ (b ∪ c)
a.Intersect(b).Intersect(c)       // the common volume of all three
solid.UnionAll(s1, s2, s3)        // when there is no natural receiver

// Smooth seams. k is the blend size; for RoundMin, k IS the fillet radius (verified at a 90° seam).
a.SmoothUnion(solid.RoundMin(2.5), b)     // circular fillet, radius 2.5
a.SmoothUnion(solid.ChamferMin(2.5), b)   // 45° chamfer with 2.5 legs
a.SmoothCut(solid.PolyMax(2.0), pocket)   // smooth-max for cuts and intersects
a.SmoothIntersect(solid.PolyMax(k), b)
// Other kernels: PolyMin, ExpMin, PowMin. A large k near a thin feature deforms the feature.
```

A cut that has to go all the way through sizes its tool from the target, never by hand:

```go
body.Cut(shape.Hole(3.2).TranslateX(12).Through(body, v3.Z(1), 1))   // profile, target, direction, pad
```

`Through` extrudes the profile to span the target's bounding box along the direction with `pad` proud at each end, so the tool cannot leave a skin and the length cannot go stale when a thickness changes. The profile lies in the plane perpendicular to the direction, and the tool is centred on the target along that direction only, so a profile positioned before the call keeps its position.

Cut in one variadic call, `body.Cut(t1, t2, t3)`, never chained: it is faster (the field is sampled once) and it reads as one operation. Smooth blends on non-exact fields (a difference, a twist) can close narrow gaps silently; confine the blend to a region, or check the gap with a probe afterwards.

## Transforms cheat-sheet

```go
s.Translate(v3.XYZ(1, 2, 3))   s.TranslateX(5)   s.TranslateXY(2, 3)   s.TranslateXYZ(1, 2, 3)
s.RotateX(90)   s.RotateY(90)   s.RotateZ(45)            // degrees, right-hand rule, see conventions
s.RotateAxis(v3.XYZ(1, 1, 0), 30)                        // axis need not be unit
s.RotateToVector(v3.X(1), v3.Z(1))                       // rotate so the first direction lands on the second
s.Scale(v3.XYZ(1, 0.5, 1.5))   s.ScaleUniform(1 / 0.996) // about the WORLD ORIGIN
s.MirrorXY()  s.MirrorXZ()  s.MirrorYZ()                 // flip Z, flip Y, flip X
s.Center()                                               // bounding-box centre to the origin
s.ZeroZ()                                                // minimum Z to 0: on the build plate
s.Transform(m)                                           // any solid.M44; builders: Translate3d, RotateZMatrix, Scale3d, ...
```

## Positioning cheat-sheet

The canonical way to place parts. Every solid has 27 named anchors on its bounding box; align them to other anchors or to absolute coordinates without bbox arithmetic.

```go
// Anchor selectors (return AnchoredSolid). Names are axis directions: Front = -Y, Back = +Y, Left = -X, Right = +X.
s.Top() s.Bottom() s.Right() s.Left() s.Back() s.Front()     // 6 faces
s.TopRight() s.BottomFront() s.FrontLeft() ...                // 12 edges
s.TopFrontRight() s.BottomBackLeft() ...                      // 8 corners
s.AnchorAt(x, y, z int)                                       // each in {-1, 0, +1}

// Relative placement (anchor -> anchor) returns a Placement. Two readings of every verb:
// receiver moves (On / Above / Below / RightOf / LeftOf / Behind / InFrontOf)
cap.Bottom().On(body.Top()).Union()
boss.OnTopOf(plate.Top()).SmoothUnion(solid.RoundMin(2))
m.Right().LeftOf(host.Left(), 1).Solid()                      // .Solid() = the moved part alone, no boolean
// receiver stays (Attach / AttachAbove / AttachBelow / AttachRight / AttachLeft / AttachBehind / AttachInFront)
body.Top().Attach(cap.Bottom()).Union()
plate.Top().AttachAbove(boss.Bottom(), 2).Union()

// Cutting: the chain's subject is what is kept. Start from the body, pass the positioned tool to Cut.
body.Cut(pocket.Top().On(body.Top()).Solid())
body.Cut(hole.Bottom().Above(body.Top(), 2).Solid())

// Sugar on *Solid
s.OnTopOf(t.Top())   s.UnderneathOf(t.Bottom())   s.RightOf(t.Right())   s.LeftOf(t.Left())
s.InFrontOf(t.Front())   s.BehindOf(t.Back())   s.Inside(t)             // bbox centre on bbox centre
t.AttachOnTop(s, gap)   t.AttachUnderneath(s, gap)   t.AttachRight(s, gap)   t.AttachLeft(s, gap)
t.AttachBehind(s, gap)   t.AttachInFront(s, gap)

// Absolute (return *Solid)
s.Top().AtZ(50)          s.AnchorAt(0, 0, 1).At(v3.XYZ(0, 0, 50))
s.BottomAt(0)  s.TopAt(50)  s.LeftAt(-20)  s.RightAt(20)  s.FrontAt(-10)  s.BackAt(10)   // FrontAt pins the MIN-Y face
s.CenterAt(v3.XYZ(0, 0, 25))
s.OnTopOf(plate.Top().ShiftY(-4))                         // Shift moves the anchor point, not the solid

// Placement finalisers
.Union() .Add()   .Cut() .Difference()   .Intersect()   .SmoothUnion(min)   .SmoothCut(max)   .SmoothIntersect(max)   .Solid()

// 2D: the same anchor selectors and the receiver-moves verbs, +Y is up. No Attach* verbs, no Behind/InFrontOf,
// and the escape hatch is .Shape(), not .Solid().
```

### Layouts (positions for `.Multi(...)`)

```go
peg.Multi(layout.Polar(20, 6)...)                    // 6 on a circle, first on +X
peg.Multi(layout.PolarArc(20, 5, 0, 90)...)          // 5 spanning a 90° arc, endpoints inclusive
hole.Multi(layout.Grid(10, 10, 4, 4)...)             // nx*ny grid centred on the origin
post.Multi(layout.RectCorners(80, 50)...)            // 4 corners
peg.Multi(layout.BoxCorners(v3.XYZ(20, 10, 5))...)   // 8 corners
post.Multi(layout.Line(v3.X(0), v3.X(60), 4)...)     // n equally spaced, endpoints inclusive
// 2D: layout.Polar2, PolarArc2, Grid2, Line2, RectCorners2. layout.SetGridLimit guards against a runaway copy count.
```

### Reach-for guide

- `.Translate(v)` — a literal offset unrelated to other geometry.
- `anchor.At(p)` — land a specific edge or corner on a literal point.
- `anchor.On(target)` and the sugar verbs — relative to another part. Use the `Attach*` reading when the chain's subject should be the assembly, not the part being added.
- `BottomAt(z)` and friends — flush a face against an axis plane.
- `layout.X` + `.Multi(...)` — copies in a regular pattern.

### The recipe pattern (preferred style for assemblies)

Ingredients at the top, method at the bottom. Top: bare primitives assigned to named variables, no transforms, no booleans. Bottom: one fluent expression that positions and combines them with anchor verbs and layout helpers.

```go
body := solid.Cylinder(50, 25, 4)
pocket := solid.Cylinder(40, 20, 0)
foot := solid.Cylinder(4, 4, 0.8)
cap := solid.Cylinder(4, 25, 1.5)

cap.OnTopOf(
    body.Cut(pocket.Top().On(body.Top()).Solid()).
        OnTopOf(foot.Multi(layout.Polar(18, 4)...).Top()).Union().Top(),
).Union().STL("out.stl", 5.0)
```

Reach for it when there are several parts to assemble; do not force it on a single primitive or on procedural geometry. The lantern cookbook is the canonical worked example.

## Modifiers cheat-sheet

```go
s.Shell(t)            // hollow, closed on every face, and the wall is CENTRED on the original surface: t/2 in, t/2 out, so the part grows by t/2
s.Offset(d)           // every surface along its normal; positive outward
s.Shrink(d)  s.Grow(d)  // the same operation as Offset with the sign fixed; no faster, no slower
s.Elongate(v3.X(10))  // insert a 10 mm straight section: total X extent grows by 10
s.Correct(0.7)        // scale the field down where a twist or scale-extrude makes it overstate distance (fixes holes in renders)
s.Voxel(cells, nil)   // pre-sample the field on a grid: the 3D speed-up for expensive fields (Cache() is 2D only)
s.StraightenBelow(z0) // replace everything below z0 with the z0 cross-section extruded straight down: a lead-in for a twisted feature
s.WithBounds(box)     // report a larger bounding box without changing the field: for Gyroid, and for bbox coupling between parts
s.Split(plane)        // (kept side, other side) — the print-in-two-pieces primitive
```

Two of these deserve a second read. **`Shell` makes the part bigger**: a 20 mm sphere shelled at 2 spans 22 mm. If a lid or socket was sized against the outer dimension, shrink first or shell then trim. **`Shrink`, `Grow` and `Offset` are exact only on exact fields.** On a `TwistExtrude`, `ScaleExtrude`, `Screw` or `SweepHelix` the field understates distance, so a `Shrink(2)` removes about 3 mm of real material and the factor depends on the twist rate. Offset the 2D profile before sweeping instead; that is exact.

To make a cup or an open box: shell, then cut away the face you want open.

## Patterns cheat-sheet

```go
s.Array(nx, ny, nz, v3.XYZ(sx, sy, sz))       // regular grid starting at the receiver
s.RotateCopyZ(n)                               // n copies around Z; the receiver's own angle is inferred and re-centred, so a pre-rotated source is fine
s.RotateUnionZ(n, solid.RotateZMatrix(step))   // n explicit copies at any step, including partial arcs; the identity copy is included
s.LineOf(p0, p1, "xxx.xxx")                    // along a line: 'x' copy, '.' skip
s.Multi(v3.XYZ(...), v3.XYZ(...))              // variadic offsets; pass a slice as s.Multi(pts...)
s.Orient(base, directions)                     // copies aligned to direction vectors
// Smooth-blended: SmoothArray, SmoothRotateUnionZ. 2D: methods on *Shape — sh.RotateCopy(n), sh.RotateCopyAt(n, deg), sh.RotateUnion(n, step)
```

`RotateCopyZ` folds space, so it costs one field evaluation per query however many copies there are, but the source's angular extent must be less than 360°/n; wider sources panic with a message pointing at `RotateUnionZ`. **Do not use `RotateCopyAtZ` on a source you have already rotated**: it assumes the source sits at 0° and renders nothing, with no error. Rotate first and use `RotateCopyZ`, or use `RotateUnionZ`.

## Cross-sections (3D to 2D)

```go
slice := shape.SliceAt(part, plane.AtZ(0))    // *shape.Shape; also plane.AtX, plane.AtY, plane.At(origin, normal), plane.XY/XZ/YZ
slice.ToSVG("section.svg", 200)
slice.ToDXF("section.dxf", 200)
slice.Extrude(1).STL("section.stl", 8)        // a slice you can look at in 3D
half := part.CutPlane(origin, normal)         // keeps the side the normal points to: a cutaway for inspection
```

## Output

```go
part.STL("part.stl", 5.0)                  // cellsPerMM: mesh density, independent of part size
part.STL("part.stl", 5.0, 0.9, 0.02)       // decimation: ANY ratio in (0,1) enables it; the 4th argument, max deviation in mm, is what sets the triangle count (default 0.05)
part.ThreeMF("part.3mf", 5.0)
shape2d.ToDXF(path, cells)   shape2d.ToSVG(path, cells)   shape2d.ToPNG(path, w, h)   // PNG is a distance heatmap, not an outline
```

Render time scales as cells cubed. Iterate at 1 to 2 cells/mm, finish a 50 mm bracket at 5, a 10 mm gear at 15 to 20. Tiny parts hit `solid.MinCells` (32) so a 1 mm sphere still renders.

## Traps, ranked by what they have cost

Each of these has produced a wrong part in the record this file comes from.

1. **Assuming what the person left out.** Print orientation, nozzle size, which surfaces are visible, what a bought part's package looks like, which face is "the bottom". These cost more revisions than every API trap combined. If a fact changes the geometry and the description does not settle it, ask before building.
2. **Size words on a curved feature.** "Long" on a boss that follows an arc means along the arc, not along Z. "4 wide" on a lug can be a chord or an arc. Name the feature's own axes before you pick numbers.
3. **A word with two readings.** "Chamfer on the bottom" can mean cut into the part or add a support wedge under it. "Triangular" can mean a cross-section or a corner gusset. Naming the standard form (buttress thread, teardrop hole, corner gusset, labyrinth seal) resolves most of these; when it does not, ask.
4. **Frames.** A part is modelled with Z up, printed on its side, used upside down. "Up" for an overhang is up in the print frame. Rotate into the print frame before auditing overhangs, and say which frame every direction word is in.
5. **`FrontAt` pins the minimum-Y face.** See conventions.
6. **`ExtrudeRounded` grows the footprint** by the round, so a gear profile extruded with round 0.4 is 0.8 mm oversize and will not mesh at the computed centre distance. Use `Extrude` for anything that mates.
7. **`Shell` straddles the surface**; the part grows by half the thickness.
8. **`Shrink`, `Grow` and smooth blends on twisted or scaled fields** overshoot or close gaps. Work on the 2D profile before the sweep.
9. **`Intersect(a, b)` is a ∩ (a ∪ b)**. Chain for a true multi-intersection.
10. **`RotateCopyAtZ` on a pre-rotated source is empty**, silently.
11. **Coincident faces.** A union across a shared face is safe. A subtraction whose face lies exactly on the body's face leaves a zero-thickness skin; make cutting tools 1 to 2 mm longer than the body, always, or let `Shape.Through` size the tool from the target for you.
12. **A flat face welded into a curved one** meets it only at the midline; the edges float. Extend the flat part past the chord into the curved body.
13. **Bounding-box placement of a composite part** puts a feature at the bbox, not at the feature. Place relative to the real face (probe for it) when the part has protrusions.
14. **Renders lie by omission.** A single view hides a sealed window, a floating body, a mirrored stamp. Look from six directions and section through the feature under discussion; better, probe.
15. **Features nobody asked for.** Tapers, fillets, clearances, lead-ins and vents added "to be helpful" are the ones that fail. Build what was asked; list what you chose not to add.

## Verify before you claim

Every failure in the record that a model caught itself, it caught by measuring, not by looking harder at the code. The `validate` package makes each measurement one line, in a test or in a throwaway `main`. The pattern that worked, every time: build, probe the points that encode what the person asked for, sweep anything that moves, audit printability in the print frame, and turn every bug you find into a probe that stays.

```go
import "github.com/snowbldr/fluent-sdfx/validate"

// Ask the field directly. Negative is inside. Takes the fluent vector type.
d := validate.At(part, v3.XYZ(10, 0, 5))
ok := validate.Inside(part, validate.Cyl(12.5, 120, 3.5))     // cylindrical coordinates: r, degrees, z

// Named probes encode intent; the report line names the failure.
validate.RequireProbes(t, part, []validate.Probe{
    validate.In("boss1-height-kept", v3.XYZ(0, 12.5, 4.8)),
    validate.Out("boss1-tip-removed", v3.XYZ(2.75, 12.5, 3.5)),
    {Name: "wall-at-least-1mm", P: v3.XYZ(9, 0, 5), Inside: true, Margin: 1.0},
})
// [ok] boss1-height-kept (0.000, 12.500, 4.800) want=inside got=inside sdf=-0.200
// [FAIL] boss1-tip-removed (2.750, 12.500, 3.500) want=outside got=inside sdf=-0.250

// Measure, do not derive.
r, _ := validate.SurfaceR(part, 45, 3, 0, 30)                 // radius of the surface at angle 45°, height 3
w, _ := validate.WallThickness(part, v3.XYZ(9, 0, 5), v3.X(1), 20)
gap, _ := validate.Opening(part, v3.XYZ(0, 0, 7), v3.Z(1), 20) // clear span through a void
validate.RequireNear(t, "bore", r, 8.0, 0.05)

// Two parts: clearance, contact, congruence. Reads one part's field on the other's surface.
g := validate.Clearance(plug, socket, 8)                        // g.Min, g.Median, g.P95, g.Max, g.MinAt
validate.RequireClearance(t, plug, socket, 8, 0.2)
validate.RequireCongruent(t, rebuilt, original, 8, 0.02)

// Motion: a static fit check passes, only the sweep finds the collision.
poses := validate.ScrewPoses(5, 360, 6)                          // 5° steps, one turn, rising 6 mm
validate.RequireSweepClear(t, lug, body, poses, 8, 0.3)
validate.RequireSweepBlocked(t, flippedKey, socket, validate.LinearPoses(v3.Z(-1), 0, 10, 1), 8, 0.5) // anti-flip

// Printability, in the frame you will actually print: rotate first, min-Z is the plate.
validate.RequireOverhangArea(t, part.RotateX(90), 8, validate.OverhangOptions{MaxDeg: 45}, 2.0)
validate.RequireStandsOn(t, part, 0, 0.01)

// Moldability along a draw direction: can a mold half pull away from this?
// The direction is an argument, so a part is scored along candidates without being rotated.
rep := validate.Moldability(part, v3.Z(1), 5, validate.MoldOptions{})
rep.Moldable()                                                   // no undercuts, nothing under-drafted
validate.RequireMoldable(t, part, v3.Z(1), 5, validate.MoldOptions{}, 2.0)  // last argument is the mm² budget

// Regression guards: a refactor that should change nothing, proven pointwise; a change that should be local, proven local.
validate.RequireIdentical(t, before, after, validate.GridPoints(before.Bounds().Box, 1), 1e-6)
validate.RequireUnchangedOutside(t, before, after, editedRegion, 8, 0.01)

// Handedness, which no render shows reliably.
validate.RequireHelixHand(t, thread, 1.25, 12, validate.RightHand)

// Physical iteration: coupons cut from production geometry, self-labelled; assembled fit checks to look at.
coupon := validate.Coupon(part, keepBox, 8)                      // panics if it is not one body
coupon = validate.Dimples(coupon, 3, at, normal, along, 1.5, 0.4, 3)
validate.FitCheck("out", "assembly", parts, origin, v3.X(-1), 8)  // writes assembly.stl and a cutaway
fmt.Println(validate.Manifest(parts, 4))                          // name, bbox, size, volume, bodies

// Mesh-level, when you need the mesh: watertight, volume, components.
validate.RequireWatertight(t, part, 5)
validate.RequireOneBody(t, part, 5)
validate.RequireVolumeNear(t, part, 5, 12500, 0.02)
```

The two moldability verdicts are different repairs and are reported separately. An **undercut** face looks back against the draw, or points along it but sits under a lip that the ray march finds — either way the part needs another mold part. An **under-drafted** face releases in principle but is shallower than `MinDraftDeg` (default 1°), and the repair is to taper it. Faces lying in the parting plane at the back of the draw are the mold's opening, not undercuts, which is what lets a flat-backed part pass in one piece; `OpenFaceTol` defaults to one mesh cell and switching it negative audits the part as a closed two-part mold instead.

To look at a part, render it from the standard views: `go run github.com/snowbldr/fluent-sdfx/tools/inspect part.stl` writes six PNGs (four isometric, top, bottom) with f3d, opaque and unlabelled, so a person or a model can read them. For a section, cut the solid with `CutPlane` and inspect that STL.

A rule from the record worth keeping: probes verify what you thought to check, renders catch what you did not think of. Use both. And a self-check by the same agent that wrote the code is weak evidence; a probe is not.

## Parametric helpers (`obj` package)

All take a parameter struct and panic on invalid input.

```go
obj.Bolt(obj.BoltParms{Thread: "M8x1.25", Style: "hex", TotalLength: 30, ShankLength: 6})
obj.Nut(obj.NutParms{Thread: "M8x1.25", Style: "hex", Tolerance: 0.1})
obj.Washer3D(obj.WasherParms{Thickness: 1.5, InnerRadius: 4.5, OuterRadius: 8.5})
obj.Panel3D(obj.PanelParms{Size: v2.XY(80, 50), CornerRadius: 4, HoleDiameter: 3.2,
    HoleMargin: [4]float64{6, 6, 6, 6}, HolePattern: [4]string{"x.x", "x", "x.x", "x"}, Thickness: 3})
obj.Standoff3D(obj.StandoffParms{PillarHeight: 12, PillarDiameter: 6, HoleDepth: 8, HoleDiameter: 2.5,
    NumberWebs: 4, WebHeight: 4, WebDiameter: 10, WebWidth: 1})   // HoleDepth > 0 tapped hole, < 0 support stub
obj.InvoluteGear(obj.InvoluteGearParms{NumberTeeth: 24, Module: 2, PressureAngleDeg: 20,
    Backlash: 0.05, Clearance: 0.2, RingWidth: 6, Facets: 16})    // pitch diameter = teeth × module
obj.GridfinityBase(obj.GridfinityBaseParms{Size: v2i.XY(2, 1), Magnet: true, Hole: true})
obj.PanelBox3D(obj.PanelBoxParms{...})                             // returns []*solid.Solid
obj.ImportSTL(path, 20, 3, 5)                                      // an existing mesh as a solid: a reference to compare against
```

`Thread` names come from the sdfx thread table: `"M8x1.25"`, `"M5x0.8"`, `"unc_1/4"`. `shape.ThreadLookup(name)` shows the dimensions. Also there, with 2D siblings for most: `Hex3D`, `HexHead3D`, `ChamferedCylinder`, `CounterBoredHole3D`, `ChamferedHole3D`, `CounterSunkHole3D`, `BoltCircle3D`, `CircleGrille3D`, `KeyedHole3D`, `Keyway3D`, `Knurl3D`, `KnurledHead3D`, `EuroRackPanel3D`, `Pipe3D`, `PipeConnector3D`, `Servo3D`, `Spring3D` (and `SpringLength`), `Geneva2D`, cams, `GearRack`, `Angle3D`, `TruncRectPyramid3D`, `DrainCover`, `Arrow3D`, `Axes3D`, and a tab system for splitting a part into keyed printable pieces: `NewStraightTab`, `NewAngleTab`, `NewScrewTab`, `AddTabs`. The full list with signatures is in `llms-api.txt`.

## Common idioms

- **Cutting tools longer than the body, always.** `shape.Hole(d).Through(body, v3.Z(1), 1)` sizes the tool from the target; by hand, pad by 1 to 2 mm. An exact-height hole leaves a skin.
- **Shrinkage compensation** at the very end: `part.ScaleUniform(1 / 0.996)` for a 0.4 percent shrink, before `.STL`, after every placement (scale is about the origin).
- **Mating gears** share `Module` and `PressureAngleDeg`; centre distance is `(N1 + N2) × Module / 2`. Extrude them with `Extrude`, not `ExtrudeRounded`.
- **Text**: `shape.Text(...).Cache()` before you use it twice.
- **A part that must go together one way**: make the keys asymmetric, and prove it with `RequireSweepBlocked` on the flipped assembly.
- **A refactor that must not change the part**: `RequireIdentical` on a grid of points, at 1e-6.

## A complete example

```go
package main

import (
    "github.com/snowbldr/fluent-sdfx/obj"
    "github.com/snowbldr/fluent-sdfx/solid"
)

const shrink = 1.0 / 0.996

func main() {
    gear := obj.InvoluteGear(obj.InvoluteGearParms{
        NumberTeeth: 24, Module: 2, PressureAngleDeg: 20,
        Backlash: 0.05, Clearance: 0.2, RingWidth: 6, Facets: 16,
    }).Extrude(4)                                          // not ExtrudeRounded: that would add 0.8 mm to the diameter

    hub := solid.Cylinder(8, 8, 0.5).TranslateZ(2)
    shaft := solid.Cylinder(20, 3, 0)                      // longer than the part: no skin
    setScrew := solid.Cylinder(20, 1.25, 0).RotateY(90).TranslateZ(4)

    part := gear.Union(hub).Cut(shaft, setScrew).ScaleUniform(shrink)
    part.STL("gear.stl", 6.0, 0.9, 0.02)
}
```
